I give my students a one-month plan. In week one, they keep the original audio and switch the subtitles to English. That's all. In week two, they rewatch something they already know very well. A cartoon, a favorite film. Because they know the plot, they can stop worrying about the story and listen to the language. And in weeks three and four, they turn the subtitles off for ten minutes a day. Most of them tell me they feel exhausted at first. Their eyes and ears are working together for the first time. I tell them it's completely normal, and that it gets easier after a week or two. And it always does.

People ask me what I do, and I say I write the words at the bottom of the screen. But there's a difference between subtitles and closed captions. Subtitles show what people say. Closed captions also describe the sounds. Door slams. Music playing. Someone laughing in another room. Captions were first made for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and that's still the main reason they exist. But today lots of other people use them. Modern films have a lot of background noise, the dialogue is fast, the accents are different. Even my mum, who's never had a problem with her hearing, watches everything with captions on now.

My kids are learning Spanish, and my secret weapon is cartoons. But not new ones. I take the cartoons they already know and love in English, and I switch the audio to Spanish. At first they complained. Now they don't even notice. Why does it work? Because they already know the story. They know what happens next, so they're not stressed about the plot, and they pay attention to the words. And they rewatch the same episodes again and again, which is exactly what you need to pick up a language. Last month, my son used a Spanish expression from his favorite cartoon in a real conversation with our neighbor. I couldn't believe it.
